name: Scripted sessions that end right and requirements met
purpose: A scripted session answers every turn and ends cleanly, and a person working with the AI while it works can watch, stop, resume, steer, see helpers, approve and read the result on two harnesses.
record: One number: the share of scripted-stdin sessions that come out right (every turn reaches the front door in order, nothing a person typed is lost, a question is answered by the next line, the wanted text is shown, the session ends cleanly), balanced with time by [balance.terminal_session]; weights and budgets fixed in esoi.toml before any arm was scored. Kinds of case, as case sources of one component: turn, command, ask, exit (evaluation/terminal_session/build_cases.py). First stage, model-free: a stub front door answers each line from the case, so the check costs nothing. Later stages (a real offline run of the whole hub, a person's trial) rise in fidelity and keep this number. Added case kind attend (live helper reported by the loop itself, a stop during a slow model call, a tree of solution workers, the structure toggled and opened, ceilings, the soft-limit and stop-decision lines, the end of a run, a follow-up that continues the session, a harness switch, the no-goal prompt and the Representative, beside the earlier scenarios) (evaluation/terminal_session/sessions.py): scripted sessions on the hub's own loop (a scripted completion behind the loop runner) and on a fake that keeps the stream runner's contract, each scored by named checks against requirement ids X1 to X23 of docs/explanation/working-with-the-ai-while-it-works.md; the share of cases right is the number, and per-requirement shares are reported. Added case kinds on 2026-11-10: documented (nine scenarios taken from what the reviewed terminals document and from the consumer's requirement tests, driven with raw stream-json lines and typed events that know no arm: a refused command shows its reason, a helper's file counts as changed, a run is not met while a helper works, the first seconds show a start, a message is queued until read, a helper's question names the helper, the answer's markdown is rendered, a stopped run keeps its work and names the resume command, a run that changed nothing says so) and pty (the real entry point: `ahohs work` on a pseudo-terminal, python pty, with a real fast-tier session on the Claude CLI login, nine scenarios: complete run, Escape then resume, steer, structure open, follow-up, harness switch, a refused command, a long markdown answer, input history; a key is sent when a file appears, a run is over when its worker process is gone, what the person saw is the text the terminal printed; evaluation/terminal_session/pty_stage.py). Run the real stage with `--max-calls`. The real stage runs with --max-calls (esoi run terminal_session --impl <arm> --record --max-calls 40).
disadvantages: Few invented sessions against a stub front door: it shows the loop holds, not that a person finds the screen clear. The pseudo-terminal stage has no terminal emulator, so what stays on a full-screen screen (scrollback, a menu, the mouse) is not judged, only the text the terminal printed and the files; a person's trial is still the later stage. Scripted harnesses prove the contract, not that a real model's run feels right; a person's trial on a real terminal is the later stage.
cascading_conditionals: free [sample=full | real=no | gate=all-pass | when=the arm was recorded on the same cases]

name: Terminal screen as drawn (presentation) after the correctness gate
purpose: A terminal arm is ranked by how its screen is drawn for a person working with the AI, once it does what the requirements say: every update shown once, the current step in view, finished work kept across a stop, a correction shown as sent then taken up, a risky step waiting with its preview, a complete closing report, rows that fit, calm redraw, readable contrast, plain output when not a terminal, whole key hints, a quick first output, and every control reaching the harness with an acknowledgement or a plain notice that it is not available. It ensures the arm that opens bare `ahohs` is chosen on the screen a person sees, not on a script that cannot see it.
record: Layer 1, the number: the weighted share of the named checks passed, over the same scripted sessions on a scripted fake harness (no model), each drawn at 80x24 and 120x40 and read back from the emulated screen: the terminal emulator pyte (LGPL-3.0, an evaluation-only dependency) for an arm that writes to a stream, Textual's run_test for a Textual arm (drawn by the arm's own application and transcript where it has one: a capture hook in presentation_of, added on 2026-11-11 when polished_session was first scored, with no check or weight changed), and an external client in a pseudo-terminal through the same emulator. Checks (evaluation/terminal_presentation/checks.py, each tied to requirements X1 to X33): each update shown once (no duplicate row, nothing in both the live region and the scrollback), current step visible, stop then resume keeps work, correction sent then taken up, risky step waits with its preview, closing report complete, no row wider than the terminal and no sideways scroll, repaints at most 10 a second with at most 4 cursor jumps each, contrast 4.5:1 (3:1 for decoration), plain when not a terminal, key hints present and whole, first output within one second, and the control round trips (stop, resume, steer, approve, refuse reach the harness and show an acknowledgement; a control the surface cannot do is shown as not available). Revision 2, 2026-11-11: the owner used the terminal at a narrow width and said it still looked handwritten, which revision 1 had scored as right, so nine checks were added from what he saw and a third size, a narrow one of 56 columns, joined the other two: no raw markdown marker on screen, no internal event vocabulary (read from the renderers' own event and step kind names, plus the lifecycle labels the shared rules hide), the answer's words once, no figure line with an empty segment, the resume command whole on one logical line, the header carrying the product's full name and fitting the width, no stray leading padding, cost at cent precision, and the goal drawn as the person's message; the run he pasted is a scenario (pasted_run) that the old look, kept as a deliberately broken arm, fails on every one of the new checks and the renderers now pass. The weights of the new checks were fixed in esoi.toml before any arm was scored on them, every arm is re-scored on revision 2, and rows recorded under revision 1 describe the earlier set of checks. Two scenario changes ride with it and are stated, not hidden: the stop scenario now waits in the stopped state as a person's would (the stop was acknowledged on a screen that resumed in the same instant), and its acknowledgement also accepts the line that says how to resume, because the header now shows state as a glyph; and a command that must stay whole is not counted as a row wider than the screen. A case scores the weighted share of the checks that applied; weights and their reasons are fixed in esoi.toml [balance.terminal_presentation.check_weights] before any arm was scored; the balanced score is [balance.terminal_presentation]. The protocol ceiling column is reported beside it and is not scored: hub information a surface cannot show at all (the structure tree on request, spend against ceilings, who the AI acts for, a correction shown as taken up, stopping one helper) is a miss there and not a rendering fault. Layer 2, advisory and never the gate: a model judges six fixed frames (start, mid run, waiting, stopped, finished, narrow) as text grids against a frozen checklist of 15 yes or no items drawn from Nielsen's ten heuristics, the Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (CHI 2019) and clig.dev, quoting the frame for every yes, three runs and a majority, arms blinded and shuffled, tier by the role deliverable_judge, read with its miss rate on a calibration set of 12 frames with injected defects (evaluation/terminal_presentation/judged). The harness and the calibration set are built. The tie-break rule, written on 2026-11-11 before the judge was run on anything: layer 1 ties when two arms fail the same checks (none, or the same ones) and show the same protocol-ceiling column, and a balanced-score difference that comes only from the cost and time terms is not a layer 1 win. Only a layer 1 tie may be broken by layer 2, and only after the judge proves reliable on the calibration set: at most 2 of the 12 injected defects called fine (at most 2 misses) and at most 1 of the 12 clean frames called a failure (at most 1 false alarm), judged by majority of three runs. The thresholds are a judgement, set from the set's size: one pair is 8.3 points, two misses is a sixth of the defects, and a false alarm is stricter than a miss because it blames an arm for a fault it does not have; 12 pairs cannot prove reliability (the interval around two misses in twelve is wide), so passing only allows the judge to speak, and the next rule keeps it from deciding on noise. A layer 2 difference breaks a tie only when one arm's share of checklist items judged yes (majority of three runs, per item) exceeds the other's by more than the larger of the two arms' run-to-run spreads (the range of the share over the three runs); otherwise the incumbent, the arm selected in the records, stays. If the judge misses the thresholds, layer 2 is not run on any arm and the rates are reported. Calibration run on 2026-11-11 (the balanced tier of the role deliverable_judge, three runs, majority, spend about a dollar as the CLI reports it on the subscription login; the calls and the figures are in judged/layer2_results.json): three defects called fine and two clean frames called a failure (rates in judged/layer2_results.json), so the thresholds were not met, layer 2 was not run on any arm, and every layer 1 tie stays with the incumbent. The misses were no-key-hints, no-preview and no-outcome; both false alarms were on the item that an update is shown only once, which the judge read as failed on the clean mid-run and finished frames (the same helper appears as a row and in the agents list), so that item or those frames may be ambiguous; the thresholds were not changed after seeing this. The correctness gate is metric-terminal-session (its scripted sessions on two harnesses): an arm that fails any of its cases is not ranked on presentation. Revision 3, 2026-11-11: three checks (risky step waits with its preview, key hints present and whole, goal as the person's message) judge the fact on screen through labels the arm declares (`screen_labels`: allow, refuse, stop, the person's marker), so a third-party screen is not failed for its wording; the declared label must be on the screen at the right moment (an empty or absent one fails, which the baseline `false_labels` proves), the control round trips prove each label does what it says, and an arm that declares nothing is held to the hub's shared words as before. No weight changed, contrast is unchanged, and every arm was re-scored. A scenario from a real run (real_run, from the recorded events of a real native session, anonymised) joins pasted_run: the real harness sends its interim note as the answer cut with three dots and three figure updates before the finish, which the scripted run did not, so answer-once now sees the answer shown twice that the owner saw on the Textual arm; the shared rule now holds interim notes until a row that draws something and drops what is part of the answer by comparing normalized text. Revision 4, 2026-11-12: the owner asked that a person can go in and out of sub-agents and message or stop them while they work, to any depth and without the screen getting worse, so ten checks (X34 to X38, weights fixed in esoi.toml before any arm was scored) read the screen of a scripted run with helpers nested to depth 1, 2 and 4 (agents_scenarios.py: each helper listed with its state, entering and leaving it, a message and a stop aimed at one agent and asserted on the harness side by agent id, a breadcrumb and one key up a level at every depth, a finished helper enterable with its result shown once, and the screen at depth 4 within one tolerance stated once of the screen at depth 1: content starting at most 2 columns further right, header and footer rows within 1, every key label shown at depth 1 still shown, entering at most 0.25 seconds slower and at most 1.5 times as slow) plus one recorded real fast-tier run over made-up notes (real_agents), with each arm declaring the keys and words it uses (agent_keys and agent_labels, like screen_labels) and two deliberately broken arms (indents_per_depth and message_to_parent) that must fail. Revision 5 (2026-11-12) added five checks from the owner's real run (no bookkeeping tool lines, a failed command as one muted plain line, a ceiling stop said once, no clipped or doubled words in the footer at 56, 80 and 120 columns, and labels capitalised on every scenario screen of every arm, the exemptions being file names and paths, commands a person types, key names, the agent's own text and wrapped continuation lines) in the feed_noise and ceiling_stop scenarios; the external clients are not run on them. Revision 6 (2026-11-12): the owner tried every terminal arm and said the metric missed the richness of the screen (the stock opencode client the richest, with a command palette, many commands, tabs, going into and out of agents and a different presentation per kind of update; the Mistral Vibe based arm the cleanest; the polished arm the best design and colour; Toad full but needing a large screen; the reference terminal none of the richness), which revisions 1 to 5 had scored as level. Six capability checks were added (X44 to X48, weights fixed in esoi.toml before any arm was scored, thresholds in evaluation/terminal_presentation/capabilities_scenarios.py) in the scenario capabilities and run for every arm, the stock clients included, as a probe of the arm's own screen: the arm's discovery action is pressed (the help line of a hub terminal, the palette of the stock opencode client filtered by a word, the footer, palette and sessions screen of Toad in a pseudo-terminal) and what the screen then shows is read back: a list of at least 5 rows that were not there before, at least 12 rows in all, sessions listed with a way to resume, tabs or a session switcher, going into a helper and back (a hub terminal is driven through its own keys, a client is read through its surface), and at least 4 different markers among the rows for a read, an edit, a command, a command that did not work and a helper. The diff body and the plan are not in the hub's event vocabulary yet, so they are not scored; the marker is read from the screen's text, so colour is not seen. The owner's verdicts are a separate stage of the cascade, human trial evidence: the component terminal_trial reads an append-only ledger (evaluation/terminal_trial/human_verdicts.csv: who, when, arm, aspect, strength or limit, the reason in the person's words, the source), one case per aspect, and the stage requires it (requires=terminal_trial:1:1): an arm with a recorded limit is not selectable until a later verdict replaces it. A later verdict is a new row (the latest per arm and aspect is read), a new aspect is a new case, and nothing is edited. The selected arm is whatever the decision function gives; no one's preference sets it.
disadvantages: Layer 1 reads the screen of a scripted session, not a person: it cannot say whether the screen is clear, only whether named, checkable faults are absent, so two arms can tie on it and the person's trial stays the later stage. The checks are the owner's requirements restated, so an arm built to them is not tested against a fault nobody listed. Contrast assumes a dark default terminal background (a cell with no colour of its own is judged against black) and reads SGR faint (SGR 2) as half intensity, which cannot be known: the ECMA-48 definition is only decreased intensity, and published reports differ (some terminals halve the intensity, others show no change at all; https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/terminal-wg/specifications/-/issues/27, https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/vte/-/issues/2462, https://github.com/zellij-org/zellij/pull/1803, https://bugs.kde.org/show_bug.cgi?id=480843; secondhand reports, not read in any terminal's source), so the check judges the worst case and an arm that avoids faint for informative text cannot fail it; the Textual capture reads Textual's compositor, an internal of Textual, so a Textual release can change it; the flicker bound is on the repaints a stream arm writes and does not apply to Textual's differential renderer (not applicable, left out of the share); one scripted harness cannot show how a real model's run feels. The weights are judgement fixed in advance with reasons, not fitted. Layer 2 is advisory because published studies find model-judged usability evaluation unreliable (Guerino et al. 2025, arXiv 2506.16345: it found only a small share of the issues experts found, with false positives; Zhong et al. 2025, arXiv 2507.02306: more issues than experts on app screenshots, but weak on conventions and across screens, and on screenshots of graphical apps, not terminal grids), so it can only order arms layer 1 ties on, after its miss rate is known, and never overrides layer 1. Revision 6 disadvantages, stated and not weighted: the capability probes read the screen's text, so a stock client's richness is shown only through what its palette and rows say, not through its colour or its feel; a capability that a client has but this metric did not drive (Toad's own keys for going into a helper) is read as absent; the thresholds (5, 12, 4) are judgement, set before scoring; the marker check cannot tell two different colours on one glyph. The human trial stage is one person's verdicts on one day, a count of aspects that person named, so an arm he did not comment on has earned nothing there and an arm he commented on negatively is blocked until a later verdict replaces it; a verdict stays evidence of that arm as it was when he tried it, so an arm's code change does not expire it. Obtainability is a disadvantage of the stock opencode client that this metric does not weigh: it is a separate program that is not bundled (the hub cannot ship it), its terminal interface is of a major version whose server API is unversioned and moves between releases (only version 2.2.7 is tested, and a newer release on the path is a different product line with another command line), and the person must install and pin it on their own; the arm reports itself unavailable and the best measured arm that can run stands in when the client is missing.
cascading_conditionals: layer1 [sample=full | real=no | gate=competitive | requires=terminal_trial:1:1 | when=the arm passed every case of metric-terminal-session (esoi run terminal_session --impl the arm) so it is ranked on its screen only once it does what the requirements say; free, no model; run on the arm and its rivals on the same cases; arms tied here are ordered by the protocol ceiling column, then by layer 2 only after its calibration miss rate is recorded; human trial evidence (kind: human feedback, who and when and why on every row) enters as the component terminal_trial (evaluation/terminal_trial: an append-only ledger of verdicts a person gave after using each arm on a real terminal, one case per aspect, a strength earning the case and a limit failing it) and is required here: an arm with a recorded limit is not selectable until a later verdict replaces it, and the decision function reads the strengths on record beside the screen probes that measure the same things; nobody's preference sets selected; no arm is run live just to fill a row] > common [real=no | requires=terminal_trial:1:1 | when=every arm on the cases that every arm can be driven through, the third-party clients included (esoi run terminal_presentation --impl the arm --only presentation-watch,presentation-steer,presentation-stop_resume,presentation-approve,presentation-refuse,presentation-capabilities --record; an arm already run on the whole set reuses its rows): a stock client cannot be driven through the hub-word scenarios (helper hierarchy, feed noise, ceiling stop, the stop of one helper) and a case with nothing to check scores zero in layer1, so layer1 cannot compare it with the hub terminals; this stage compares all arms on the same cases and takes the human trial requirement above, so a recorded limit blocks an arm here too; record the common set last for each arm, since the newest row of the arm decides the case set it is compared on]
command: esoi run terminal_presentation --impl live_session; esoi run terminal_presentation --impl textual_session; esoi run terminal_trial --impl live_session; esoi run terminal_session --impl live_session
